paras: The pursuit of Alex Jackson by a lynching party took place at Brooksville, Florida, in May 1888, after Jackson, a Black man, was accused of shooting and killing Lucinda Berry, a Black woman. The lynching party and the sheriff's posse both hunted him, but neither caught him, and he was later captured at Ocala and jailed. The New York Sun presented the manhunt as a 'race' between the lynchers and the sheriff.

According to the reports, there had been trouble between Jackson and Berry for some time, and she had recently sworn out a peace warrant against him. The Sun's dispatch described Jackson as 'a prominent negro politician'.

Jackson was accused of entering Berry's room and shooting her in the back, killing her instantly, and then fleeing to the swamps. The papers dated the shooting differently: a dispatch dated May 17 said 'this morning', the Savannah Morning News said Wednesday, May 16, and a reward notice gave May 14. A lynching party set out after Jackson, while the sheriff, 'unusually active', led a posse of his own.

N. B. Rhodes of Brooksville offered a reward of $25 for the arrest of Jackson, described as dark-brown, about six feet tall and usually carrying a hickory stick. Jackson was captured at Ocala on a Friday, apparently May 25, by the Florida Railway and Navigation operator and placed in jail. The Morning News reported that the lynchers and the sheriff 'failed to get the murderer'.

A Black man named Shiffield was arrested as an accessory to the murder, but at his examination the state's evidence failed to connect him with it and he was discharged. No report of Jackson's trial appears in the coverage.

The New York Sun ran the Brooksville dispatch under the headline 'Race Between a Sheriff and Lynchers' and predicted 'the chances in favor of the lynchers'. The Savannah Morning News followed the case in brief items in its Florida column on May 18, 22, 28 and 30, noting that 'The parties are colored'. Neither paper commented on the lynching party, which both treated as an expected part of the manhunt.
The Morning News's capture item says 'Both parties were colored', which most likely refers to Jackson and Berry, as in its earlier notice, so the race of the lynching party is not clear.

bases: A lynching party pursued Jackson after the shooting but did not catch him; he was jailed at Ocala, so the episode is a threatened lynching during a manhunt (A1, A2, A4).
A 'lynching party' set out after Jackson on an accusation of murder, but it 'failed to get' him and he was jailed at Ocala, so no one was killed (A1, A2, A4).

The New York Sun dispatch and the Savannah Morning News Florida column agree on the shooting and the lynching party's pursuit, with differing dates and details, and a later Morning News item reports the pursuit and the capture (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: Brooksville dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: Jackson shot Berry 'this morning' and fled to the swamps; a lynching party and the Sheriff's posse were both after him, 'with the chances in favor of the lynchers.'

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News Florida column
accounts.gist: The shooting took place Wednesday and a lynching party started after Jackson; a later item reported that the lynchers and the Sheriff failed to get him and that he was captured at Ocala.

framing.detail: The Sun ran it under 'Race Between a Sheriff and Lynchers', treating the lynching party as an expected rival to the posse without comment on its legality.
The Morning News gave brief Florida-column notices, calling Jackson 'the murderer' in its capture item.

versions.value: 'This morning' in a dispatch dated May 17

conflicts.note: The May 17 dispatch and the May 18 'Wednesday' notice point to May 16 or 17; the reward notice's 'May 14' may be a misprint, and the May 28 'last Wednesday' looks carried over from an earlier local report.
Variants of one name; the reward notice says he 'generally calls himself A. J. Jackson'.
